title: Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18)
hook: a tentmaking couple teach eloquent Apollos more accurately, aside from the crowd
tomorrow: why would new believers set fire to their own books?

segments.voice: Paul began from an altar with no name, and told Athens that God is not far from each one of us. Now he moves on to Corinth, and finds two people who work with their hands.
screen: `NOT FAR FROM EACH ONE.` → `ON TO CORINTH.`

segments.voice: A typo on the big screen, mid-presentation. Do you call it out, or catch the speaker after? Acts has an answer. In Corinth, Paul meets a couple, Aquila and his wife Priscilla, and "by their occupation they were tentmakers," his own trade, so he stays and works beside them. Later, in Ephesus, a gifted preacher named Apollos gets something partly wrong, in public. The ones who set him right are that tentmaking couple, and they do it away from the crowd.
screen: `A TYPO ON THE BIG SCREEN.` → `BY OCCUPATION, TENTMAKERS.` → `AWAY FROM THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Today's question: how do you tell someone they've got it wrong without crushing them? Here's how Acts tells it. Apollos is "a certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures." He's getting a great deal right. One piece is missing: he knows "only the baptism of John." Priscilla and Aquila hear him in the synagogue, and they don't stand up and fix him in front of the room. "They took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly." Took him unto them: aside. More perfectly: not starting him over, adding what was missing. Apollos takes it, and goes on to help many believers. Now a neighbor. Judaism has a commandment for this exact moment. Leviticus, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour." Jewish teachers call it tochachah, loving correction, and the Talmud reads the end of that verse as a limit: correct him, but not in a way that shames him. That's the one to tell a friend tonight: both traditions say speak up rather than stew, and guard the other person's face while you do it. The honest difference: in Judaism this is a mitzvah, a commandment, with rabbis weighing how and when; Acts gives no rule here, only a story, and what the couple adds is teaching about Jesus, which Jews and Christians hold differently.
screen: `MIGHTY IN THE SCRIPTURES.` · `THEY TOOK HIM UNTO THEM.` · `A NEIGHBOR: SURELY REBUKE.` · `SPEAK UP, BUT DON'T SHAME.` · then, large: `MORE PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and recall a time someone set you right kindly, out of everyone's view. Stay with what made it easy to hear: their tone, their timing, the fact that nobody else was watching. If you pray, you can ask for a kind tongue.
Priscilla and Aquila. Two tentmakers who took a gifted preacher aside and showed him the way of God more perfectly.
Hold on to this: more perfectly, which means adding what's missing, not starting over. Day done.

notes: The index hook says 'in their home'; Acts 18:26 says only 'they took him unto them'. The lesson says 'aside' and the hook field says 'aside from the crowd'. Confirm.
The KJV of Acts 18:26 reads 'Aquila and Priscilla'; the lesson keeps the index title's order. Manuscript differences in the order of the names are left out under the claims rule.
'Goes on to help many believers' paraphrases Acts 18:27 ('helped them much which had believed through grace'). Confirm.

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): the neighbor is Judaism. Leviticus 19:17 quoted from JPS 1917 ('Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart; thou shalt surely rebuke thy neighbour'); confirm exact wording and punctuation. The Talmud (Arakhin 16b) reading of the end of the verse as a limit on rebuke, so that it doesn't shame, is paraphrased; a Jewish scholar should confirm the citation and wording.

The shared point (speak up rather than stew; guard the other's dignity) and the honest difference (in Judaism a commandment with rabbinic limits; in Acts a story with no rule, and the content added is teaching about Jesus, which Jews and Christians hold differently) are given without ranking. Confirm both are fair to each tradition.
Christians also read Leviticus 19:17 as scripture; the lesson presents it here as Judaism's own commandment in its own translation, which is accurate but a Keeper may want that overlap named.
